newsitem.title: UK: Airlines face crucial week over open skies pact.
newsitem.headline: Airlines face crucial week over open skies pact.

text.p: The airline world faces a crucial week as British and U.S. officials reopen their "open skies" talks, and Europe sets the scene for hearings on the British Airways/American Airlines alliance.
British transport officials will meet U.S. counterparts next Tuesday in Washington for three days of talks to try to clinch a deal on liberalising the transatlantic airline market.

An open skies pact is just one precondition for the BA/AA alliance to be cleared, but the EU has stressed that it will not consider this factor as part of the European Commission's review of the pact until a deal is signed, sealed and delivered.
British and U.S. industry figures said on Friday they expected little more than agreement on technical issues with no major breakthrough on "open skies" in this round.
Separately major airlines headed by BA and American will send representatives to a series of private European Commission hearings on Monday and Tuesday about the planned alliance.
A senior commission official said on Friday the hearing would hear testimony from BA and American as well as rival airlines from Europe and the U.S that are opposed to the planned alliance.
On the subject of open skies, airline industry sources were cautious about their expectations.
A spokesman for BA said: "We'll make further useful progress. The two governments are close on a range of issues. But it won't lead to an open skies deal this time."
One U.S. airline spokeswoman agreed, saying: "We expect no outcome this time either."
The talks would focus on the "nitty gritty technical issues," she said.
While the U.S. government wanted to keep the BA/AA deal out of the open-skies equation, she said, the British government had the opposite view, wanting to link the two.
The last set of open skies talks were held in London and ended without a breakthrough.
Airline sources who attended that meeting said talks had been hampered because there was still no verdict from British competition authorities on the BA/AA deal.
Ironically the verdict from Britain's competition watchdog, the Office of Fair Trading, came just minutes after the open skies round was wrapped up.
One airline industry source said this time round a key issue for the British side could be a dispute reconciliation procedure to be established to protect smaller airlines under open skies.
Airlines remained upbeat about a deal being sealed at some point, despite the currest sluggish pace. "It's moving in the right direction," said one.
